objective: Test whether first-half high three-point accuracy predicts second-half regression; establish data coverage before inference
selection: Convenience sample from existing SharpEdge postmortems with explicit first- and second-half 3PT makes/attempts; NOT random or exhaustive; no historical league-wide baseline
inclusion: both halves numeric 3PM/3PA with 3PA>0, halftime known
findings: High-shooting subset includes Houston (42.1% to 45.5%) and Memphis (54.2% to 42.9%); one rose, one fell.
Memphis scored more points in 2H (70) than 1H (66) despite lower three-point percentage, so 3PT regression alone did not imply scoring regression.
Golden State increased from 39.3% 1H to 52.4% 2H and scored 61 after halftime versus 63 before; 1H is below predeclared 40% cutoff.

Sample is selected post hoc, only 5 team-games, lacks pace/possessions, opponent strength, injury rotation, attempt-mix, rest and a proper comparison baseline; no meaningful predictability test or p-value is justified.
Regression toward a population shooting rate is a statistical expectation under a stable process, not evidence that a profitable second-half betting signal exists.
conclusion: NOT DEMONSTRATED: no reliable evidence from this convenience sample that similar first-half shooting profiles predict second-half scoring regression or offer market edge.
next_required_test: Build season-scale team-game halftime dataset with 3PM/3PA both halves, possessions, lineup/rotation, rest, score, opponent, timestamped halftime odds; chronological walk-forward benchmark vs baseline and no-vig market; evaluate probability calibration and EV out of sample.
